name: 1000 Physical per 1 Logical
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Thousand-to-One Tax
lesson.summary: Quantum error correction hides one reliable logical qubit inside roughly a thousand noisy physical qubits, and that ratio is the single most consequential number in scaling a quantum computer.
lesson.body:
Every physical qubit built today is noisy. Even the best superconducting and trapped-ion qubits have error rates around one in a thousand operations, and most algorithms that would actually be useful, like simulating a novel catalyst or breaking modern encryption, require billions of quantum operations to run correctly. If a single error can spoil the whole computation, an error rate of one in a thousand is nowhere close to good enough. Quantum error correction is the answer, and it works by encoding one unit of protected quantum information, called a logical qubit, across many physical qubits, so that errors on individual physical qubits can be detected and corrected without ever directly measuring, and thus destroying, the fragile quantum state being protected.

The catch is that this protection is expensive. The leading error-correction scheme, the surface code, arranges physical qubits in a two-dimensional grid and repeatedly measures local parity checks between neighbors. The larger the grid used to encode one logical qubit, the more exponentially suppressed its logical error rate becomes, but the number of physical qubits needed grows roughly with the square of that grid's size. Given today's typical physical error rates, researchers commonly land on a rule of thumb: roughly a thousand physical qubits are needed to encode one logical qubit reliable enough for long algorithms. That number is not a law of physics. It shifts with the code used, the physical error rate achieved, and how many operations the algorithm needs to survive, and better codes or lower physical error rates can push it down. But as an order-of-magnitude estimate, it has held up across many independent analyses.

The consequence is easy to see with a simple estimate. A fault-tolerant algorithm that needs 1,500 logical qubits, a modest number for serious chemistry or cryptography problems, would need on the order of 1.5 million physical qubits just to hold the error-correcting codes themselves, before even counting the extra physical qubits needed to prepare the special resource states, often called magic states, that most useful gates require, which often adds a comparable amount of overhead on top.

This is also why raw qubit counts in press releases can be misleading. A chip with a thousand physical qubits sounds impressive next to earlier generations, but under the thousand-to-one rule it might correspond to roughly one logical qubit, or in practice today, none at all, since no group has yet run a full fault-tolerant logical qubit through a real algorithm at meaningful scale. Current machines mostly demonstrate error correction in small proof-of-concept form: a handful of logical qubits, held together just long enough to show the error rate goes down as the code grows, not to run a program of any real value.

Understanding this ratio is the starting point for understanding why the resource requirements of a genuinely useful quantum computer look so different from the qubit counts being built today.
